newsitem.title: USA: Dlr surges vs European currencies on Buba comments.
newsitem.headline: Dlr surges vs European currencies on Buba comments.

text.p: Buoyed by strong U.S. economic data and supportive comments from a German official, the dollar surged Monday to near two-year highs against the mark, the Swiss franc and the French franc.
The dollar also jumped higher against the yen, moving above the 114 threshold for the first time in almost a month and coming close to matching a 42-month late-October high of 114.92 yen.

"There was just outright dollar buying across the board and it just snow-balled on itself because a lot of people who hadn't expected the move were not positioned for it," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar closed at 1.5545 marks, about one-and-a-half pfennigs better than Friday's close of 1.5390, but slightly down from a 23-month session high of 1.5590.

The U.S. currency surged to close at 1.3215 Swiss francs versus 1.3043 on Friday, after reaching a 23-month high of 1.3280 in afternoon trade. Against the French franc, the dollar ended at 5.2730, after touching a 22-month high of 5.2820 French francs.
Against the Japanese currency, the dollar ended the session at 114.55 yen, up from Friday's close of 113.87.
Traders said the impetus for the dollar's strong move came from Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and November manufacturing data from the National Association of Purchasing Management.
The monthly NAPM index rose to an unexpectedly strong 52.7 reading in November against 50.2 in October, suggesting continued firm growth in the U.S. manufacturing sector.

Meanwhile, the Bundesbank's Issing told a bankers' forum in Germany on Monday that one of the possible effects of the approach of Europe's single currency union was a shift out of the deutschemark into dollar-denominated investments.
"It was the Issing remarks more than anything else that got us started," said Kevin Lawrie, global foreign exchange manager at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank.
The remarks reinforced a dollar rally kindled late last week and over the weekend, when French and German central bank officials began talking actively about their desire for a stonger dollar.

In order to meet tough convergence criteria for Economic and Monetary Union, many European countries have been forced to observe strict fiscal and monetary discipline despite struggling economies. As a result, many European Union members are hoping that weaker currencies can fuel export-driven growth, and keep their economies on an even keel.
"Every single central banker and politician in Europe seems to want a stronger dollar," said Robert Fullem, assistant vice president at Natwest Bank Plc.
In addition to the European push for a firmer dollar, Fullem said that strong demand for surging U.S. stocks and bonds has also played a role in the U.S. currency's rise.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar was nearly unchanged at Canadian $1.3507, against C$1.3503 in late Friday trading. The British pound was slightly lower at $1.6810, down from $1.6825 last week.
